eval_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the levying of monitoring fees on the individual applicants’ wages involved violations of Articles 9, [DATE_TIME], and 14. The Court declared the application admissible with respect to the five individual applicants and inadmissible insofar it concerned the Swedish Construction Industries (Sveriges Byggindustrier) (hereinafter “the Industries’) The case was heard in public in [LOCATION] (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr [PERSON], Ministry of Industry, Employment and Communications, and (b) the applicants. The relevant local branch of the Union in the instant case was the [LOCATION] branch, Byggettan. The local branch had the right to inspect on a continuous basis wage conditions by measuring piecework (ackordsarbete) and result work ([PERSON), as well as monitoring time-based work (tidlönearbete). If inspections were carried out in accordance with the collective agreement, the local branch was entitled to reimbursement of the costs involved on the basis of a fee of 1.5% of the worker’s wages. An out-of-court settlement was reached on [DATE_TIME] to the effect that it applied to all workers belonging to a trade union other than the Union. Two of the applicants were heard by the Labour Court. The case concerned fees for monitoring the wages for [DATE_TIME] work. The company complied with their requests, stopped paying the fees to Byggettan and did not provide it with the above-mentioned wage information concerning the applicants. The Union disagreed with the Industries, arguing that the monitoring fees could not be seen as tantamount to forced membership of the Union. The system of monitoring fees did not involve a compulsion to join a trade union. Also, the applicants had not expressed any ideological reasons for their unwillingness to contribute to the monitoring work. They submitted that they opposed the deductions because they did not think the work was of any use to them. The Union claimed that a ban on the levying of monitoring fees on unorganised workers’ wages would violate the positive rights of its members. The inspection work was strictly separated, economically and otherwise, from the other activities of Byggettan. The Labour Court stated that there was no reason to come to a different conclusion in the instant case as to the nature of the monitoring work. The court concluded that the levies of fees on the wages of members of the Syndicalist Union for monitoring work carried out by another trade union involved a violation of those worker’s positive freedom of association, as they would have to resign from their own organisation. The Labour Court initially concluded that the monitoring fee deductions did not entail membership of the Union. It found that no pressure had been exerted to compel the applicants to join the Union against their will. It referred to the European Court’s case-law and drew the conclusion that only the core of the negative freedom of association was protected under Article 11 of the Convention. It said that a person must have been subjected to a certain measure of force or at least strong pressure to join an organisation in order to give rise to a violation of Article 11. The court went on to state that, while the applicants, through the fee deductions, contributed to the general activities of the union, they were not treated any differently from Union members as concerns the monitoring. Court concluded that all the above considerations indicated that the deductions did not breach the applicants’ rights under the Convention. As the fee was not tantamount to forced membership of the Union and had not influenced or forced the applicants to join the Union, the company had been obliged to make a deduction from their wages in accordance with the collective labour agreement. Court could not find that the monitoring fee was intended as a measure to pressure them to joining the Union – the court could not finds that it had any such coercive effect. The court concluded that the deduction was in line with the terms of the collective Labour Agreement and was not a breach of the applicants' rights.
